articles.title: UK government forced to admit it issued Apple a secret encryption order
articles.summary: UK government forced to admit it issued Apple a secret encryption order

top_comments: Apple has significantly weakened its security assurances in a way that is arguably deceptive. They used to say nobody can access your data, not even Apple. Now they say Apple cannot access your data. People will point out that your key is created on your device, lives on your device, and never leaves your device, but that is just your key. Your key is likely a KEK (key encryption key) that opens another key (not “your” key, let’s call it the actual key) that your data is secured with. There can be other parties (UK government) with their own KEK that opens a copy of the actual key. In this scenario, Apple can have no access to a KEK that opens the actual key, but they are forced to make the wording change they did, if they want to stay honest.I say the statement is arguably deceptive because it presents the same feel of assurance that the old one did, to most people.Note John Ternus in a recent event (WWDC keynote if I recall correctly) used the old wording. I think this was a slip-up (I’d hate to think it was a calculated lie posing as a slip-up).

Primary source: https://investigatorypowerstribunal.org.uk/judgement/1-mr-vi...The key finding seems to be that the media learned of the technical capability notice through confidential security briefings, and not a leak (“one of those irregular verbs”).The contents of the note remains secret for now.

articles.title: The 98% Slot Machine: How Paid Advertising Became an Extraction Tax
articles.summary: The 98% Slot Machine: How Paid Advertising Became an Extraction Tax

top_comments: This analogy doesn't hold at all. Casinos are engineered for the house to win and the customer to lose because the casino is paying the customer directly. They are disincentivized to let the customer win. If the customer always won, the casino goes out of business very quickly.Ad auctions are completely different, since they are just a marketplace. A customer's (advertiser's) win comes from a third party, and the point of the ad platform is to connect that third party to the customer. The ad platform would love to be able to make every single customer win all the time. Although, if they did that, it would create a lot more demand and even out the ROI with increased ad prices. But that's not the "evil ad platform" engineering the customers to always lose in the way casinos do, that's simply basic supply/demand economics.COI disclaimer: My current job is a small part of an ads platform on a website you have heard of. I dislike ads but realize they are a necessity for running some parts of the internet.

I've seen some posts on X where they celebrate mobile apps making 7 digit MRR but then you look at their net profit is like only mid 5 digits after taxes and ad spend and Apple's cut.One developer in particular shared that he was spending $580k to make $650k before taxes and app store fees and you realize that apple is double dipping, it's an insane level of taxation on the developer to take on all the risk and its gamified so that you really can't penetrate big niches without it being a spending contest.

I use to think we lived in an enlightened age, where we have now learned that we need to use scientific reasoning and analysis to make decisions. It is what lifted us up from superstition and folk tales.But society, still, collectively, falls for snake oil, over and over again.This topic was talked about in 2019. https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=21465873Freakanomics did a great podcast about if Internet Advertising actually works. https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47906485Anyone that has an interest in the topic should listen (or read) about what Steve Tadelis did in the 2012 timeframe. He was an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley, and then worked at eBay, where he led the famous experiment on Google ad effectiveness.
